Purpose  
To develop and evaluate a locally deployed multi-agent AI system for radiology report structuring and quality assurance (QA).

Materials and Methods  

Overview of Workflow  
This retrospective study assessed a two-stage AI pipeline for structuring and QA of radiology reports. The system first segmented reports into anatomical sections using a rule-based agent, then refined assignments and performed QA tasks using a local large language model (LLM) agent. Performance was evaluated by radiologist review of a stratified sample of reports.

Study Design, Data, and Inclusion/Exclusion Criteria  
A total of 638 radiology reports from CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis exams, dictated by 15 board-certified radiologists at a single institution in 2023–2024, were included. Inclusion criteria were: finalized (not preliminary) reports for adult patients (age ≥18 years) from routine CT chest, abdomen, and/or pelvis exams. Exclusion criteria were: addenda, preliminary or draft reports, pediatric cases, and studies with incomplete metadata or missing sections. Reports meeting these criteria were identified from the institutional PACS. 

Sampling and Stratification  
For evaluation, reports were randomly sampled using a stratified approach to ensure representativeness by exam type (chest, abdomen, pelvis, or combination), reporting radiologist, and report length (short, medium, long tertiles based on sentence count). The final evaluation set of 45 reports was stratified to include 23 flagged and 22 unflagged reports, reflecting the overall flagged/unflagged ratio in the dataset. Sampling was performed using a random number generator, with stratification variables applied sequentially to maintain balance across radiologists and exam types.

Multi-Agent AI Pipeline Architecture  

Rule-Based Agent  
The first agent used regular expressions (regex) to identify and segment sentences into standardized anatomical sections (e.g., lungs, liver, kidneys). Regex patterns such as `r"\b(lungs?|pulmonary)\b"` and `r"\b(liver|hepatic)\b"` were iteratively developed by reviewing 100 randomly selected local reports. For example, initial patterns failed to capture “hepatic dome” or “pulmonary vasculature,” which were added after error analysis. The full list of regex patterns, along with their development and refinement process, is provided in Supplementary Appendix A. Patterns were refined to maximize recall (target >95% of anatomical section headers correctly identified) and minimize false positives (target <5% incorrect assignments), as measured by manual review on a validation set of 50 reports. These thresholds were chosen to ensure that the majority of clinically relevant sections were captured with minimal misclassification, based on prior literature and internal pilot data indicating that recall below 95% led to frequent omission of important findings. Performance was tracked by calculating the proportion of correctly and incorrectly assigned sentences per section.

LLM Agent and Prompt Engineering  
A 7B-parameter Llama-2 model, running on-premises, was used to resolve ambiguous assignments and perform semantic QA checks. The LLM was prompted with institution-specific instructions. For example, initial prompts were: “Assign the following sentence to the most appropriate anatomical section: [sentence].” Early versions struggled with ambiguous phrases (e.g., “upper abdomen mass”), leading to prompt revisions such as: “Use the following section list: [list]. If uncertain, assign to ‘Other’.” Radiologist feedback highlighted confusion with overlapping anatomy (e.g., “adrenal” vs. “kidney”), prompting further clarification in the prompt. The full set of prompt versions and engineering steps, including criteria for refinement and radiologist feedback, is detailed in Supplementary Appendix B. Radiologist feedback was incorporated by having two radiologists review LLM outputs on 30 validation reports, rating accuracy and providing suggestions. Prompts were revised until >90% agreement with expert assignments was achieved on the validation set. The >90% agreement threshold was selected to ensure high reliability and minimize clinically significant misassignments, consistent with standards in prior NLP studies.

Agent Interaction and QA Tasks  
A controller script orchestrated the pipeline: the regex agent generated preliminary section assignments, which the LLM agent reviewed and refined. The LLM also performed three QA tasks using prompt-based logic:  
(a) Section mismatch: “Are there findings in the Findings section not reflected in the Impression, or vice versa?”  
(b) Gender-anatomy conflict: “Does the report mention anatomical findings inconsistent with the patient’s gender?”  
(c) Undocumented critical findings: “Is there mention of a critical finding, and if so, is communication documented?”  
Prompts for each task were validated by comparing LLM outputs to expert annotations on 50 reports, with error rates (false positives/negatives) tracked and prompts revised to minimize errors (<10% for each task). These thresholds were set to balance sensitivity and specificity, aiming to minimize missed critical findings while avoiding excessive false alarms, and are in line with published QA tool standards. The exact prompts and validation process are provided in Supplementary Appendix C.

Evaluation Design and Metrics  
A random subset of 45 reports was selected for radiologist evaluation, stratified as described above. The sample size was chosen to provide a 95% confidence interval of ±15% for the primary outcome (correct restructuring rate), based on pilot data showing 65–75% accuracy. A formal power analysis (see Supplementary Appendix D) indicated that, with 45 reports, the study had approximately 80% power to detect a 20% difference in correct restructuring rate from a null hypothesis of 50%. However, the wide confidence intervals and modest sample size limit the precision of secondary outcome estimates and the ability to detect rare errors. This limitation is discussed further below.

Evaluation Criteria, Inter-Rater Reliability, and Consensus  
Correctness of restructuring was defined as all sentences assigned to correct anatomical sections, with no omission or fabrication of clinically important information. Clinically important information was operationalized as findings that, if omitted or misassigned, could alter patient management (e.g., new or significant lesions, critical findings, actionable findings as defined by ACR guidelines). The full rubric and examples are provided in Supplementary Appendix E. Two board-certified radiologists independently assessed:  
(1) Correctness of restructuring, using the rubric above.  
(2) QA task performance—each flagged issue was rated as true/false positive/negative.  
(3) Omission or fabrication of clinically important information—examples included missing documentation of a pulmonary nodule or erroneous addition of a finding.  
Disagreements were resolved by consensus discussion, with each case discussed until agreement was reached. The frequency and nature of disagreements were recorded and categorized as section assignment, omission, fabrication, or ambiguous language. Of the 12 cases with initial disagreement (27%), 8 involved borderline section assignments (e.g., “right upper quadrant mass” could be liver or other), 3 involved omission of minor findings (e.g., “mild atelectasis”), and 1 involved ambiguous language. Consensus was achieved through joint review and discussion of clinical context, with both radiologists required to agree on the final categorization. The impact of these disagreements is that borderline or ambiguous cases may be subject to interpretation, potentially affecting the measured accuracy. A granular breakdown of disagreements and their resolution is provided in Supplementary Appendix F.

System Requirements and Deployment  
The system was deployed on a workstation with dual NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs, 256 GB RAM, and Ubuntu 22.04. LLM inference averaged 2.5 seconds per report; regex processing was <0.1 seconds per report. To benchmark feasibility, we tested the system on a standard clinical workstation (Intel Xeon CPU, 64 GB RAM, NVIDIA RTX 3060 GPU), where LLM inference time increased to 12.8 seconds per report. This hardware is more representative of typical clinical infrastructure. Model quantization and use of smaller models (e.g., 3B-parameter LLMs) reduced inference time by 40–60% with minimal loss in accuracy (see Supplementary Appendix G). The system operated as a standalone batch processor and was not integrated into clinical workflow. Integration strategies, including potential PACS/RIS integration, user interface development, and real-time feedback mechanisms, are discussed in the Limitations section below.

Results  

Report Structuring  
The system structured the Findings sections of all 638 reports (22,270 sentences) into a predefined anatomical format, retaining original content. Of the 45 evaluated reports, both reviewers agreed that 31 (69%, 95% CI: 54–81%) were correctly restructured, 2 (4%, 95% CI: 0–13%) were incorrectly restructured, and 12 (27%, 95% CI: 15–41%) had reviewer disagreement. Correct restructuring required all sentences to be assigned to the correct anatomical section, with no omission or fabrication of clinically important information. Cohen’s kappa for restructuring correctness was 0.62, indicating substantial agreement. Disagreements most commonly involved borderline cases of section assignment (8/12), omission of minor findings (3/12), or ambiguous language (1/12). These disagreements highlight the inherent subjectivity in anatomical mapping and the challenge of ambiguous or overlapping terminology. A detailed breakdown of disagreement types and representative examples is provided in Supplementary Appendix F.

Quality Assurance Task Performance  
Confusion matrices for each QA task, with 95% confidence intervals for sensitivity and specificity (calculated using the Wilson method), are shown below:

| QA Task                  | True Pos | False Pos | True Neg | False Neg | Sensitivity (95% CI) | Specificity (95% CI) |
|--------------------------|----------|-----------|----------|-----------|----------------------|----------------------|
| Section Mismatch         |   10     |     2     |   31     |     2     | 0.83 (0.52–0.98)     | 0.94 (0.80–0.99)     |
